LAHORE, Pakistan (CNN) -- Two Pakistani television networks that transmit from Dubai in United Arab Emirates were ordered off the air Friday at the request of Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf, officials from the networks said. Pakistan's president, Gen. Pervez Musharraf, has been under pressure to lift a state of emergency. GEO-TV and ARY Digital offer a variety of programming, including news, entertainment, sports and music. Both networks had been banned from Pakistan's cable television system -- along with other networks, including CNN and BBC -- since Musharraf declared a state of emergency on November 3. This latest action prevents the two Pakistani networks from broadcasting worldwide via satellite. "This was basically our window to the world, GEO President Imran Aslan said. "In Pakistan, we've been shut down since the 3rd." The action was not wholly unexpected, but surprising nevertheless, Aslan said. "We uplink from Dubai, never having had a license to uplink from Pakistan," he said. "Dubai is a media city which seemed to be a haven and a sanctuary." Aslan said network officials have been in discussions with Pakistani government officials and "it seemed very obvious that they were going to do this. We were ready for it to a certain extent." "Eventually they decided to put their feet on the pipe, as it were." The government has made numerous demands of the network, although none of them official, Aslan said. "It's done through intermediaries," he said. "[Dulling] down the content, not having certain anchors, some of the hosts of our programs and talk shows." Musharraf's emergency order put several restrictions on the media, preventing journalists from expressing opinions prejudicial to "the ideology ... or integrity of Pakistan." Journalists are also restricted from covering suicide bombings and militant activity and could face three-year jail terms if they "ridicule" members of the government or armed forces. Almost a dozen journalists have been arrested. Musharraf has denied that his restrictions bar criticism, saying they only ask for responsibility in reporting. But last week, Pakistan expelled three print journalists for using language in an editorial that a Pakistani official called offensive to Musharraf. The editorial criticized Musharraf and the United States and Britain for continuing to support him. While many Pakistani journalists have protested the restrictions, some smaller television channels have complied with the government's restrictions. GEO and ARY have refused. "It seems most of the other channels have kowtowed in order to survive," Aslan said. Musharraf has said the emergency order improves stability and will foster peaceful parliamentary elections, which he has said he would like to see take place before January 9. The exact date will be set by Pakistan's Election Commission. Opposition leaders have accused Musharraf of declaring emergency rule to keep his hold on power and avoid an expected court ruling that would have nullified his election victory in October. LAHORE, Pakistan (CNN) — Officials at two Pakistani TV channels broadcasting out of Dubai in the United Arab Emirates said Friday that they had been instructed to stop transmitting, following a request from Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf.

Musharraf, Pakistan’s president and army general, has faced growing pressure to end the state of emergency he imposed. The two channels, GEO-TV and ARY Digital, air a mix of news, entertainment, sports and music programming.

Since Musharraf declared emergency rule on November 3, both channels had already been removed from Pakistan’s cable television lineup, along with several other broadcasters, including CNN and the BBC. The new move goes further by blocking the two Pakistani networks from sending their broadcasts around the world by satellite.

“This was basically our window to the world,” GEO President Imran Aslan said. “In Pakistan, we’ve been shut down since the 3rd.”

Aslan said the decision was not entirely unforeseen, though it still came as a shock. He explained that GEO had always transmitted from Dubai and had never held a license to uplink from Pakistan. “Dubai is a media city which seemed to be a haven and a sanctuary,” he said.

According to Aslan, network representatives had been talking with Pakistani government officials, and “it seemed very obvious that they were going to do this. We were ready for it to a certain extent.”

“Eventually they decided to put their feet on the pipe, as it were,” he added.

Aslan said the government had made many requests of the channel, though none had been formally issued. “It’s done through intermediaries,” he said, citing pressure to reduce the strength of the channel’s content and to remove certain anchors and hosts from programs and talk shows.

Musharraf’s emergency decree placed broad limits on the press, barring journalists from making statements considered harmful to “the ideology ... or integrity of Pakistan.” Reporters were also restricted in how they covered suicide attacks and militant activity. Under the order, journalists could receive prison sentences of up to three years if they “ridicule” government officials or members of the armed forces.

Nearly 12 journalists have been detained.

Musharraf has rejected claims that the rules prohibit criticism, saying instead that they are meant to promote responsible journalism. However, the previous week, Pakistan expelled three print reporters over wording in an editorial that a Pakistani official described as insulting to Musharraf. The editorial had criticized Musharraf as well as the United States and Britain for continuing to back him.

Many Pakistani journalists have demonstrated against the restrictions, though some smaller television stations have chosen to follow the government’s rules. GEO and ARY have not agreed to do so.

“It seems most of the other channels have kowtowed in order to survive,” Aslan said.

Musharraf has argued that emergency rule strengthens stability and will help create conditions for peaceful parliamentary elections. He has said he wants the vote to be held before January 9, though Pakistan’s Election Commission will determine the official date.

Opposition figures have accused Musharraf of imposing emergency rule to remain in power and to avoid an anticipated court decision that they say could have invalidated his October election win.

E-mail to a friend.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Pakistan ordering GEO-TV and ARY Digital off the air from Dubai after Musharraf’s November 3 state of emergency, including quotes from GEO President Imran Aslan and background on media restrictions.
counterfactuals.output:
**Pakistan orders GEO-TV, ARY Digital off air from Dubai after emergency rule**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Pakistan’s government has ordered two of the country’s most prominent private broadcasters, GEO-TV and ARY Digital, to halt transmissions from Dubai, widening a crackdown on the media that began after President Pervez Musharraf declared a state of emergency on November 3.

Executives at GEO said authorities in Dubai Media City, where the channel’s satellite operations are based, informed them that their broadcasts had to stop following pressure from Islamabad. ARY Digital, which also broadcasts from Dubai, was similarly taken off the air.

GEO President Imran Aslam said the move was a direct extension of the restrictions imposed inside Pakistan after emergency rule was declared.

“We have been told to shut down our transmissions from Dubai,” Aslam said. “No formal reason has been given to us, but it is obvious this is being done under pressure from the Pakistani government.”

Aslam said the channel had already been blocked inside Pakistan by cable operators after the emergency decree, but continued to reach viewers through satellite. The Dubai shutdown, he said, was aimed at cutting off that remaining outlet.

“This is not just about GEO,” he said. “This is about the right of people to know what is happening in their country.”

The Pakistani government has accused some private television stations of inflaming political unrest and undermining national security. Officials have said emergency measures were necessary to combat extremism and preserve stability, but critics say the move was aimed at silencing opposition, the judiciary and independent media.

Musharraf, who seized power in a 1999 coup, imposed emergency rule on November 3, suspended the constitution and dismissed judges who were expected to rule on the legality of his re-election as president. The government also introduced new media regulations barring broadcasts that “defame” the president, the military or state institutions.

Under the amended rules, television channels faced heavy fines, suspension of licenses and possible prison terms for journalists and executives accused of violating the code. Private news channels were pulled from cable systems across Pakistan within hours of the emergency declaration.

Journalists have staged protests in several cities, accusing the government of imposing censorship reminiscent of military rule. Police have detained media workers and opposition activists during demonstrations, while several newspapers and broadcasters have reported pressure to soften coverage of protests, court actions and opposition leaders.

GEO and ARY are among Pakistan’s most influential private networks, part of a media sector that expanded rapidly under Musharraf’s own liberalization policies earlier in the decade. Their aggressive coverage of the judiciary crisis, opposition rallies and the emergency decree made them a frequent target of government criticism.

Aslam said GEO would continue trying to resume broadcasts and would not accept censorship conditions.

“We are willing to follow the law,” he said, “but we cannot agree to become a mouthpiece. A news channel cannot operate if it is told what it may and may not report.”

The shutdown from Dubai marks a significant escalation because the broadcasters had moved key operations outside Pakistan partly to avoid domestic pressure. Media advocates said the action showed Islamabad was prepared to use diplomatic and commercial pressure beyond its borders to control coverage at home.

The government has not announced when full media freedoms will be restored. Musharraf has promised elections, but opposition parties and rights groups say a fair vote cannot take place while emergency rule remains in effect and independent television news is off the air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**LAHORE, Pakistan, Nov. 17, 2007** — Pakistan’s military-led government has intensified its campaign against independent television news by moving beyond domestic censorship and pressing authorities in Dubai to silence Pakistani broadcasters operating from the Gulf emirate, including the country’s two best-known private networks, **GEO-TV** and **ARY Digital**.

The crackdown marks a new phase in President **Pervez Musharraf’s** emergency rule, imposed on Nov. 3, under which the constitution was suspended, senior judges were dismissed or detained, opposition activists were arrested, and sweeping restrictions were placed on the press.

GEO News and ARY’s news channels, which had shifted much of their transmission operations to **Dubai Media City**, were taken off air or forced to halt live news programming after Pakistani officials objected to their coverage of the political crisis. Their entertainment and non-news services were less affected, but news broadcasts — especially talk shows featuring lawyers, opposition leaders and critics of the military government — became the central target.

Executives and journalists at the networks said the move followed direct pressure from Islamabad on the authorities in the United Arab Emirates. The government of Pakistan has accused private channels of “irresponsible” reporting, spreading unrest and undermining national institutions. Media groups say the real reason is that the channels refused to accept new censorship rules requiring broadcasters to avoid criticism of the president, the army, the judiciary installed under emergency rule, and the emergency proclamation itself.

The pressure on Dubai-based transmissions is significant because Pakistan’s private television boom had relied heavily on satellite uplinks from outside the country. GEO, ARY and other channels used facilities in Dubai to reach Pakistani audiences by cable and satellite, enabling them to broadcast with greater freedom than would have been possible under direct Pakistani licensing controls. By extending its censorship campaign abroad, the Musharraf government has demonstrated that it is prepared to use diplomatic and commercial leverage to control what Pakistanis see on television.

Inside Pakistan, many private news channels had already been blocked by cable operators acting under government orders. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority, or PEMRA, was given expanded powers under emergency regulations to suspend licenses, seize equipment and punish channels that broadcast material deemed prejudicial to “national security,” the “ideology of Pakistan,” or public order. Journalists have called the rules vague and deliberately broad.

The shutdowns have badly disrupted Pakistan’s most influential television newsroom culture. GEO News, known for aggressive political talk shows and wall-to-wall coverage of the lawyers’ movement, had become a major platform for critics of Musharraf after he suspended Chief Justice **Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry** in March 2007. ARY One World, later ARY News, also carried extensive coverage of opposition protests, legal challenges and military rule. Their broadcasts helped bring images of police baton-charges, arrested lawyers and besieged courts into homes across the country.

Musharraf’s emergency proclamation was justified by the government as a necessary response to rising militancy, suicide attacks and what it described as judicial interference in counterterrorism and governance. But the timing was widely seen as political. The Supreme Court had been expected to rule on the legality of Musharraf’s re-election as president while he remained army chief. Within hours of declaring emergency rule, the government removed judges who refused to take a new oath under the Provisional Constitutional Order and placed several under house arrest.

Opposition parties, lawyers and human rights groups say the emergency is intended to preserve Musharraf’s rule rather than restore security. Thousands of political workers, lawyers and civil-society activists have been detained since Nov. 3, though some have since been released. Former Prime Minister **Benazir Bhutto**, who returned from exile in October, has also faced restrictions and temporary detention as she called for protests against emergency rule.

The media restrictions have become one of the most visible symbols of the crisis. Pakistan’s private television networks, which expanded rapidly after Musharraf liberalized the broadcast sector earlier in his rule, had become a powerful political force. The same government that once promoted private media as evidence of democratic opening is now trying to rein it in as criticism of military rule grows.

Journalists in Lahore, Karachi and Islamabad have held demonstrations despite police pressure, often appearing with black armbands or taped mouths to protest censorship. Press-freedom organizations have condemned the closures, saying Pakistan’s emergency regulations amount to prior restraint and intimidation.

The government has said channels may return to the air if they sign a code of conduct. Broadcasters and journalists say the proposed code would effectively bar live coverage of protests, criticism of the president and army, and discussion of the dismissed judiciary.

For viewers in Pakistan, the result has been a sudden narrowing of the public sphere at a moment of national upheaval. Where television screens had shown live debates, street protests and legal challenges, many cable systems now carry blank screens, entertainment programming or foreign news channels. Some Pakistanis have turned to the internet, satellite dishes and foreign broadcasters for information, but access remains uneven.

The silencing of GEO-TV and ARY’s Dubai-based operations underscores the central contradiction of Musharraf’s emergency rule: a government presenting itself as a bulwark against extremism is using extraordinary powers against judges, lawyers, political opponents and the independent media. As the emergency continues, the battle over television has become one of the clearest tests of how far the state will go to control Pakistan’s political narrative.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**Pakistani authorities press Dubai to halt GEO, ARY broadcasts ahead of elections**

ISLAMABAD — Pakistani authorities are pressuring officials in Dubai to stop satellite transmissions by two leading private Pakistani television networks, GEO and ARY, in the latest escalation of a media crackdown ahead of national elections, journalists and media executives said.

The move follows sweeping restrictions imposed under emergency rule, including bans on international news channels such as CNN and the BBC from local cable distribution, arrests of journalists and demands that broadcasters accept strict censorship guidelines before being allowed back on air.

GEO and ARY, both of which operate broadcast facilities from Dubai Media City, have been among the most prominent Pakistani networks covering political unrest, the judiciary and opposition activity. Media executives say Pakistani officials have sought to block their ability to reach audiences inside Pakistan by targeting their overseas satellite uplinks.

Pakistani authorities have accused some private channels of undermining stability and airing material deemed harmful to national security. Broadcasters and press freedom groups say the restrictions are intended to curb independent coverage at a politically sensitive moment.

The government has demanded that television stations sign a code of conduct limiting live coverage of protests, criticism of the armed forces and judiciary-related reporting, according to journalists familiar with the directives. Several stations have resisted the conditions, saying they amount to prior censorship.

The crackdown has also included detentions and harassment of reporters covering demonstrations by lawyers, opposition activists and civil society groups. Journalists’ organizations say the arrests, combined with broadcast blackouts, have sharply narrowed the public’s access to independent information.

The dispute comes as Pakistan prepares for elections expected to determine the balance of power between President Pervez Musharraf, opposition parties and civilian political institutions. Opposition leaders and media advocates say restrictions on broadcasters could affect the credibility of the vote by limiting scrutiny of the campaign and government actions.

Officials in Dubai have not publicly confirmed whether they will comply with Pakistani requests regarding GEO and ARY. Both networks have continued efforts to maintain programming through alternative means, while viewers inside Pakistan have reported intermittent access depending on cable providers and satellite availability.

International press freedom groups have condemned the measures and urged Pakistan to restore access to domestic and foreign news channels. They say open media coverage is essential if the elections are to be viewed as free and credible.

Pakistan’s government moved swiftly to tighten control over the country’s media after declaring a state of emergency, taking several private television news channels off the air and drawing sharp criticism from journalists and press freedom advocates.

Among the hardest hit were **GEO-TV** and **ARY Digital**, two of Pakistan’s most prominent private broadcasters. Some warned that the restrictions marked a major setback for Pakistan’s relatively vibrant private media sector, which had grown rapidly in the years before the crackdown.
